blocks.text: For two years, getting better results from AI meant writing better prompts.
Longer instructions, smarter system messages, increasingly complicated frameworks. Engineers spent hours figuring out which words made an agent perform better.
That approach is starting to lose its advantage.

Andrej Karpathy's autonomous research system ran roughly 700 experiments in two days and discovered around 20 improvements. Shopify's CEO reportedly used a similar approach to improve a smaller model by 19%. Boris Cherny, the creator of Claude Code, said he had gone eight months without writing code by hand. philschmid.de
The common thread is not a better prompt.
It is a loop.
A system that gives AI a goal, lets it work, checks the result, and keeps going until the objective is reached.
Here is how these loops work, why they are becoming so powerful, and how to build your first one.
1. The engineer who ran 700 experiments
In March 2026, Andrej Karpathy released autoresearch, a small open-source system designed to automate machine learning experiments.
The architecture was surprisingly simple.
Three important files controlled the process.
train.py contained the training code the agent could modify.
prepare.py handled data preparation and evaluation.
program.md described the objective, constraints, and experimental rules.
The agent had one job: improve model performance without changing the evaluation system.
It would inspect the code, propose a modification, train for five minutes, compare the result against the previous experiment, and decide whether to keep the change.
Then it started again.
Over two days, the system reportedly completed around 700 experiments and identified roughly 20 improvements. The combined changes reduced a time-to-GPT-2 benchmark from 2.02 to 1.80 hours.
One discovery involved a missing scaling factor in the attention mechanism, something that ordinary syntax checks would never flag.
The significance was not that AI suddenly became a better researcher than Karpathy.
It was that an agent could investigate hundreds of measurable hypotheses without requiring someone to approve each experiment.
Humans get tired after dozens of unsuccessful attempts.
A properly controlled loop can keep exploring as long as its budget allows.
2. A loop is not a prompt running every hour
Most people confuse automation with autonomous iteration.
They schedule a prompt, receive an answer, and call it an agent.
But running the same instruction repeatedly does not create a useful feedback system.
A real loop has five stages:
Discover → Plan → Execute → Verify → Iterate
The agent examines the problem, chooses an approach, performs the work, evaluates the outcome, and uses that evidence to determine what happens next.
Three components make the difference.
Verification: The result must pass an objective test. A compiler, benchmark, test suite, or deterministic validation script.
Memory: The system records what was attempted, what failed, and which changes produced improvements.
Stopping conditions: The loop ends when the objective is achieved or a hard limit is reached.
Without verification, the agent can confidently repeat mistakes.
Without memory, it keeps rediscovering the same failures.
Without stopping conditions, it can consume resources indefinitely.
A loop is not useful because it runs without supervision.
It is useful because its progress can be measured without constant supervision.
3. The self-healing GitHub repository
Now imagine applying the same architecture to ordinary software development.
A developer pushes code to GitHub.
The CI pipeline detects a failing test.
Instead of waiting for someone to inspect the failure manually, an automated workflow sends the logs and relevant repository context to Claude Code or Codex.
The agent investigates the error, creates a candidate fix, and runs the tests again.
If verification fails, it examines the new output and tries another approach.
If the tests pass, it opens a pull request containing the proposed correction and supporting evidence.
A human reviews the change before merging.
This is a practical example of a self-healing repository.
The workflow does not require an enormous multi-agent system.
It needs an event trigger, a coding agent, a reproducible environment, persistent state, and an independent verifier.
The same pattern can handle dependency updates, formatting violations, reproducible bugs, and routine maintenance.
The important distinction is that the agent does not decide whether its work is successful.
The repository's verification system does.
4. Build your first AI loop with three files
The easiest mistake is starting with ten agents, multiple orchestration frameworks, and an expensive monitoring dashboard.
Start smaller.
You can organize a basic coding loop around three files.
AGENTS.md — Project instructions
Define the objective, repository conventions, permitted operations, and restrictions.
For Claude Code, the equivalent project-specific instructions can live in CLAUDE.md.
loop.py — The controller
This script invokes the coding agent, manages retries, records progress, and enforces execution limits.
verify.sh — The verification gate
This file contains the commands that determine whether the required work has succeeded.
A simplified controller looks like this:

MAX_ATTEMPTS = 10for attempt in range(MAX_ATTEMPTS):    agent.run(goal="Fix failing tests")    result = verify()    if result.passed:        print("Objective completed")        break    save_feedback(result)
This is conceptual code. A working implementation needs an agent integration, error handling, rollback support, timeouts, and persistent state.
But the architecture is already there.
The agent produces a candidate.
The verifier evaluates it.
The feedback informs another attempt.
The controller determines when to stop.
Once one supervised execution reliably produces acceptable results, the process can be connected to a schedule or GitHub event.
Get one loop working before trying to build an entire autonomous engineering team.
5. Why the verifier matters more than another agent
There is a common misconception in AI engineering.
When one model makes mistakes, add another model to review its output.
Sometimes independent reviewers help.
But two AI agents agreeing does not mean their conclusion is correct.
Imagine an agent optimizing a Python function.
It rewrites the implementation and claims a 30% performance improvement.
A reviewer examines the code and agrees that the optimization looks reasonable.
Neither opinion proves anything.
The system needs to run correctness tests and reproducible benchmarks.
If the new function produces incorrect results, reject it.
If performance decreases, reject it.
If correctness is preserved and the measured improvement is real, keep the change.
This is the principle behind Karpathy's experiments.
The agent generates possibilities.
An external evaluation determines which possibilities survive.
Better models can improve the quality of proposed solutions.
Better verification improves the reliability of the entire system.
6. The two problems that can destroy an autonomous loop
The first problem is uncontrolled execution.
An agent might attempt dozens of variations without making meaningful progress.
Every iteration consumes tokens, compute, and sometimes paid infrastructure.
A loop needs hard budgets, maximum attempt counts, and a way to detect repeated failures.
The second problem is more subtle.
Comprehension debt.
An autonomous coding system can generate changes faster than its maintainers can understand them.
Tests pass. Pull requests merge. Development appears faster.
But the gap between what the repository contains and what the engineering team understands keeps growing.
Eventually, an unexpected production failure exposes that gap.
Passing tests cannot guarantee maintainability, architectural quality, or complete security.
That is why autonomous loops should initially operate on narrow, verifiable tasks.
Authentication, payments, critical infrastructure, and irreversible operations still require stronger controls and human judgment.
The objective is not to eliminate engineers from the process.
It is to eliminate repetitive work while preserving engineering responsibility.
7. The metric that actually matters
The number of agents running is not a productivity metric.
Neither is the number of prompts executed, tokens consumed, or pull requests opened.
The useful measure is cost per accepted result.
How much time, compute, and human review did the system require to produce one verified, useful change?
A loop that generates fifty patches and gets two accepted may be less efficient than one producing five carefully verified improvements.
This is why the best starting point is rarely an ambitious autonomous development platform.
It is one annoying recurring task with an objective definition of success.
Make that task reliable.
Add memory.
Enforce a budget.
Automate execution.
Then expand.
Karpathy's research experiments illustrate what happens when AI can repeatedly test its own proposals against meaningful evidence.
The same principle can transform ordinary software development.
Prompt engineering still matters, but the competitive advantage is moving toward something larger.
Designing the environment.
Defining success.
Building verification.
Creating systems that can continue making progress without requiring another human instruction every few minutes.
A prompt tells an agent what to do.
A loop gives it a way to discover whether it actually worked.
The engineers gaining the biggest advantage are not necessarily using smarter models.
They are building better systems around the models they already have.
And while everyone else is still rewriting prompts, those systems can keep experimenting, correcting mistakes, and producing verified work long after the conversation ends.
